title: How Castles Work
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss castles: the etymology of the word from Latin castellum, where castles were built (mostly Europe, about 10,000 in Germany), their origins from ancient walled cities and early motte-and-bailey and ringwork designs, and their defensive features such as moats, drawbridges, double outer walls, shield walls, hoardings, arrow loops, murder holes, crenellations, and counterclockwise staircases. They cover the bailey, keep (formerly the donjon), great hall, chapels, wells, cisterns, dungeons, and residential living quarters. The episode also covers siege tactics (starvation sieges, catapulting diseased animals, scaling ladders, siege towers, battering rams, tunneling and fire), the decline of castles with cannon, and modern castle projects in France (Guédelon) and Arkansas (Ozark Medieval Fortress). The episode ends with a listener email from Anna about hiccup-curing superpowers.

segments.title: Opening banter and He-Man toy castle
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about the show's podcast rankings and Chuck recalls a He-Man castle toy, Castle Grayskull, and what he would tell his younger self.

segments.title: Castle etymology and origins
segments.summary: The word castle comes from Latin castellum, meaning a fortified place. Castles were mostly European, with about ten thousand in Germany, and were built mainly during the High Middle Ages. Their origins trace to ancient walled cities and early grod or ringwork designs, the bergfried watchtower, and the motte and bailey design.

segments.title: Castle defenses: moats, walls, and gates
segments.summary: The hosts describe the moat as a hallmark feature, with water or sewage or dry ditches with stakes. They cover drawbridges, double outer walls filled with rubble, and shield walls, plus wooden hoardings with arrow loops and murder holes for dropping hot liquids.

segments.title: Crenellations and counterclockwise staircases
segments.summary: Crenellations let soldiers hide behind merlons and shoot arrows. Staircases spiraled counterclockwise going up so right-handed defenders had room to swing swords, a fact tied to the word sinister.

segments.title: Bailey, keep, great hall, and castle living
segments.summary: The bailey was the open courtyard used for jousts, markets, festivals, and training. The keep, formerly the donjon, housed the lord. Castles also had chapels, a great hall, storage, residential quarters, and fireplaces in most rooms. A Scottish castle is noted as supposedly haunted after a murder during mass.

segments.title: Wells, cisterns, and dungeons
segments.summary: Castles needed self-sufficient water supplies, so they had internal wells and cisterns to collect rainwater. Dungeons were originally high in the keep and later moved below ground.

segments.title: Siege tactics
segments.summary: The hosts cover starvation sieges, where attackers surrounded a castle and waited, with negotiated surrender common. Defenders set fire to the countryside, and attackers catapulted diseased animals. Other methods included scaling ladders, siege towers, battering rams with padding against flaming arrows, and tunneling under walls to burn timber supports.

segments.title: Decline of castles, cannon, and modern castle builds
segments.summary: Cannons made castles obsolete. Earthen walls and wood forts used by colonial armies replaced them, built quickly. The hosts discuss Guédelon in France, a castle built with traditional tools and funded by tourism, and the Ozark Medieval Fortress in Arkansas, plus Hearst Castle and Medieval Times.

segments.title: Listener mail from Anna
segments.summary: Anna writes about her hiccup-curing ability and photographic olfactory memory, and a Bukowski quote. The hosts thank her and ask for listener stories and a possible future episode on burping.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts point listeners to the HowStuffWorks site for more articles on castles and other topics.
